political_impact.text: The Bogoslof reservation passed without notice or opposition, like the rest of the bird-reservation program.

legacy.text: The Bogoslof Reservation became the Bogoslof National Wildlife Refuge under the 1940 renaming of federal wildlife reservations.
Congress designated the Bogoslof Wilderness at 390 acres; the Fish and Wildlife Service now gives the island as 175 acres, its shape having been greatly modified by the 2016–17 eruption.
legacy.source: Pub. L. 91-504, 84 Stat. 1104–05; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; U.S. Geological Survey

legacy.text: Bogoslof is listed among the major Steller sea-lion rookery sites, and the Bogoslof area of the Bering Sea shelf is one of three special Steller sea-lion foraging areas in Alaska.
Bogoslof was Roosevelt's last addition to the bird-reservation system he began at Pelican Island in 1903, which grew into the National Wildlife Refuge System of 573 national wildlife refuges.

today.name: Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge (Aleutian Islands unit)
today.note: Bogoslof and nearby Fire Island lie in this unit.

today.name: Bogoslof Wilderness
today.note: Designated 1970 at 390 acres; about 175 acres today.

related.note: Pelican Island, the first bird reservation; Bogoslof was the last.

later_actions.text: Folded into the Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge.

legacy.text: Bringing office deputies in United States marshals' offices into the competitive service was absorbed into the growing merit system.

related.note: Rewrote the Department of Justice exception first set in the 1903 civil-service rules.

uncertain: Whether the Inauguration Day excusal covered the whole day or part of it, and all District of Columbia employees or only those who wished to attend, is not known; no full text has been located.

political_impact.text: The last numbered executive order Roosevelt signed; the series resumed with Executive Order 1051 on March 16, 1909, under Taft.
